name: PT Pradiksi Gunatama Tbk

frontmatter.title: Pradiksi Gunatama: a small plantation carrying a large group premium
frontmatter.summary: Pradiksi Gunatama is a sub-scale East Kalimantan palm producer that sells essentially all its crude palm oil to its controlling family's refinery. Its plantation is worth a small fraction of the market price; the rest is a concentrated-ownership premium now exposed to the exchange's high-concentration list, the free-float deadline and MSCI's standalone consultation. We rate SELL, with a target that still keeps most of the gap.
thesis: Through the cycle the plantation is worth Rp468 a share on our probability-weighted twelve-month value, against Rp8,350 in the market [S0, S24].
The gap is a regime variable, not an earnings multiple: the price is 19.5x today's fundamental value and the konglo lens closes 40.0% of the log gap in its base case [S26, S13, S16].
Earnings are real but captive: 87.7% of FY2025 sales went to JARR and a further IDR96.5bn to Kodeco, so related parties take essentially all revenue [S9, S15].
Float and collateral are the binding constraints: 7.6% free float against a rising exchange minimum, with 5.3 bn shares pledged to Bank Mandiri against the group's coal acquisition [S5, S26].
Our base case keeps most of the premium for another year, so the target sits far above value yet well below the market price [S24, S26].

catalysts.event: First free-float step of the exchange's new minimum; controller sell-down or new shares required
MSCI decision on reclassifying Indonesia as a standalone market; consultation feedback closes 30 April 2027
FY2026 audited results and the dividend declaration for the year
Conditional SPA for the group's BYAN stake; any mandatory tender offer it triggers is for BYAN, not PGUN — a PGUN tender floor would depend only on pledge enforcement
IDX high-shareholding-concentration list review and index-treatment updates
HGU expiry and the extension application under PP 18/2021

blocks.text: **SELL; twelve-month target Rp4,256, a total return of -48.9% from Rp8,350.** The target is not a forecast that the plantation is worth more than the market says; it is the engine's konglo lens working through the most likely path of a concentrated-ownership premium. Fundamental value, on a probability-weighted twelve-month basis, is Rp468 a share; today's fundamental value is Rp428, so the market pays 19.5 times it [S0, S26]. Against the twelve-month figure the premium is smaller but still double-digit. We rate the shares SELL because we cannot construct a business case, within the deck's own price range, that closes the gap [S24].

What the company owns is simple and small: a single mill and an oil-palm estate in Paser, East Kalimantan, producing crude palm oil, palm kernel and shells, with 23,354 ha planted [S4]. FY2025 revenue was IDR792.7bn and net profit IDR159.3bn [S0, S18]. Every tonne of CPO is sold to the controlling family's refinery, PT Jhonlin Agro Raya (JARR), and a second affiliate, Kodeco, takes the palm kernel flow, so the business is a captive upstream feeder rather than a price-taking exporter [S17, S18, S9].

Our variant view is not that the plantation is distressed. Volumes are recovering from the El Nino trough, the mill is profitable and the balance sheet is deleveraging [S17, S0]. It is that the equity is priced as an option on the group's capital-markets agenda rather than on its palm cash flows. The controller and three family vehicles hold effectively the whole register and public float is 7.6% [S11, S12]. A few percent of the shares set the marginal price, and the exchange has now taken the name out of the headline indices while the free-float rule and MSCI's standalone consultation move against exactly this ownership structure [S26, S22].

The most likely path is not a collapse to value in twelve months. The lens assumes the premium compresses gradually: in the base regime scenario it retains Rp2,785 of value, the bear scenario Rp848, and the bull scenario Rp10,604 [S26, S12, S6]. Weighted, that is our Rp4,256 target. Two things move the value: whether the free-float deadline is met by a sell-down (which adds supply) or by an issuance (which dilutes), and whether the group's coal-financed borrowings force the pledged stake into the market [S26, S6].

This revision changes four things. We restate the FY2025 and FY2024 D&A lines to the LK totals — bearer-plant amortisation of IDR99.0bn plus fixed-asset depreciation of IDR16.0bn — so FY2025 EBITDA is IDR339.4bn on a total-D&A basis, not the pack's amortisation-only figure [S4, F3, F5, F57]. We reset FY2026 volume and cost to the 9M2026 run-rate rather than the stale June plan [S8, S15, S10]. We end the explicit DCF at the 2033 HGU and source the extension terms [S28, F9]. And we remove the own-history legs from the multiple cross-checks and drop P/BV altogether, because the only book in the pack is the revalued equity and the own-history legs embed the premium the konglo lens is meant to measure separately [S24, S4, F48].

PT Pradiksi Gunatama Tbk is an oil-palm plantation and milling company based in Batu Engau, Paser regency, East Kalimantan, listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange since 2020 [S18, S2]. It operates one palm-oil mill with 90.0 t/h of fresh-fruit-bunch capacity and sells three products: crude palm oil, palm kernel and palm kernel shells [S18, S4]. The company also develops and manages plasma smallholder plantations around its estate [S4, S8].

The asset base is compact. Planted area is 23,354 ha, of which 18,975 ha is mature and the balance is immature block that enters production as the replanting programme matures [S4]. The HGU title covers 41,562 ha and runs to 2033 [S4, F9]. PP 18/2021 Pasal 22 allows the holder to extend the term by up to 25 years and renew it for up to 35 years, and ISAK 336 treats the extension as expected unless there is evidence it will not be obtained, which is the basis on which the accounts do not amortise the land right [S28, S4]. Inside the 41,562 ha licence, the titled but unplanted balance is the HGU less the 23,354 ha planted and less the 3,625 ha plasma estate, which sits inside the same concession as an additional block managed for smallholders [S8, F9, F7, F39]. We value the unplanted balance at its carrying value (see the valuation section) rather than at zero; the plasma estate is not PGUN's own asset and is not valued separately [S4, F39]. A single mill and a single estate mean there is no geographic diversification: all output comes from one concession in East Kalimantan, as management itself told the exchange after the forest fires [S7].

The revenue mix is dominated by CPO, with palm kernel and shells as by-products. In FY2025 CPO contributed IDR694.9bn, palm kernel IDR96.4bn and shells IDR1.3bn, for net sales of IDR792.7bn [S18]. That is a narrow product set; there is no refinery, no oleochemicals and no biodiesel of its own, so the downstream margin sits with the affiliated buyer rather than with PGUN [S18, S10].

The commercial model is a captive offtake. All CPO production is allocated to JARR, the group's refinery and biodiesel producer, and management describes the arrangement as giving certainty of absorption and stable revenue [S17, S7]. The palm kernel flow goes to Kodeco, which PGUN treats as a related party through a family and commissioner link [S9]. JARR buys from three related suppliers and its trade receivables to them are large relative to its own cost base [S10]. The company is, in substance, the upstream supply leg of the Jhonlin palm complex [S18, S10].

Strategy follows from that position. The company is replanting at a steady annual rate with a dedicated budget inside its capital-spending plan, improving agronomy and land class to lift fresh-fruit-bunch volumes, and raising mill throughput and extraction rates rather than adding new land [S10, S17]. There is no announced expansion of planted area and no downstream project of its own, so growth is yield-led and slow [S10].

Competitively PGUN is a challenger at the small end. The downstream affiliate JARR books several times PGUN's revenue, and the Indonesian plantation sector is populated by groups with estates an order of magnitude larger [S18]. PGUN's advantage is not scale or cost; it is the guaranteed buyer next door, which removes market risk but transfers pricing power to the affiliate [S17, S18].

Ownership and control sit with the Jhonlin group of Andi Syamsuddin Arsyad, known as Haji Isam. The ultimate beneficiary of the controlling shareholders is his daughter, Liana Saputri, while her brother Jhony Saputra owns one of the holding vehicles [S11, S12]. Three family entities, Araya Agro Lestari, Citra Agro Raya and Baramega Citra Mulia Persada, together hold almost the entire register; the public holds 7.6% [S11, S12]. The controller's other listed interests include JARR and the coal-logistics name TEBE, and the exchange has questioned the simultaneous price rises across those stocks [S17].

Palm oil is the world's most widely traded vegetable oil. The value chain runs from fresh fruit bunches through the mill, which produces crude palm oil and palm kernel, into refining, fractionation and biodiesel. Indonesia is the largest producer, and domestic policy — the biodiesel mandate, the export levy and the domestic-market obligation — is a larger swing factor for Indonesian producers than for exporters elsewhere. Plantation economics are driven by tree age, the fresh-fruit-bunch yield per hectare, the oil-extraction rate and the CPO price, with fertiliser and labour the main cash costs.

Our agricultural deck prices CPO at US$1,135/t for the current year, US$1,240/t next year, and a long-run marker of US$1,150/t, against a spot print of US$1,180/t [S24]. The curve is not a boom forecast: it assumes the market holds near current levels through the next two years and then mean-reverts modestly [S24]. That long-run marker, not the spot print, is the price we use to value the plantation, because a cyclical producer valued on spot earnings is valued at the wrong point of its cycle [S24, S25].

The demand driver with the clearest date is Indonesia's B50 biodiesel mandate, which the government targeted to start in July 2026 [S10]. JARR has been increasing the share of internal CPO in its biodiesel feedstock and lifting plant utilisation in anticipation, which directly supports PGUN's offtake [S10]. The policy is supportive but not unqualified: its timing has depended on technical trials, industry readiness and funding, and management's own language is conditional [S10].

Regulation cuts both ways for a producer that sells entirely at home. Because PGUN sells CPO domestically, the export levy and the export-tax wedge fall on the exporter, not on PGUN, which is why our model carries no royalty line [S17, S4]. The trade-off is that the domestic price PGUN receives is administratively influenced and, in practice, set in a related-party contract. The replanting programme is partly a response to the government's smallholder-replanting push and the rise in fresh-fruit-bunch reference prices [S10]. The exchange's own rules on ownership concentration are now a first-order industry variable for this name: the minimum free float rose to 15.0% from March 2026 with a managed transition, and high-shareholding-concentration names have been removed from the headline indices [S26, S21].

On market structure, the industry is fragmented at the estate level and concentrated at the refinery level. PGUN is a price-taker on inputs and a contract seller on outputs: it buys third-party fresh fruit bunches alongside its own estate crop, and sells all CPO to one affiliate [S4, S18]. That is a weak position in a five-forces sense. Buyer power is extreme because there is one buyer and it is related; supplier power is moderate because plasma and third-party fruit can be sourced locally; the threat of new entrants is constrained by land permits and the long gestation of new planting; substitutes matter at the vegetable-oil level through soyoil, whose deck price has been volatile [S24]; and rivalry among producers is intense but largely irrelevant to PGUN because it does not compete for customers [S18].

The moat is contractual, not economic. There is no evidence of a first-quartile cost position: the company's cash cost is backed out of its own accounts at about the level implied by a mid-cost Indonesian estate, and its scale is too small to command procurement or logistics advantages [S4]. What protects the earnings is the offtake agreement, and that protection is only as good as the affiliate's own balance sheet and willingness to pay. The JARR receivables disclosure suggests the group's payment chain is stretched, which is a governance exposure rather than a commercial moat [S10].

External influences are the CPO price, the rupiah, the weather and policy. The rupiah matters because the deck price is in dollars and most costs are in rupiah, so a weaker rupiah flatters margins [S25, S24]. Weather matters directly: the 2025 production recovery followed the El Nino impact, and forest fires in Kalimantan in late 2026 required a formal response to the exchange even though management said operations were unaffected [S17, S7]. Policy matters through biodiesel demand and through the exchange's own rules on ownership concentration, which we treat as a first-order industry variable for this name [S10, S26].

Revenue has been cyclical and, until recently, shrinking. Net sales were IDR1,007.3bn in FY2022, IDR868.5bn in FY2023, IDR738.6bn in FY2024 and IDR792.7bn in FY2025 [S0]. The recovery in FY2025 came from a modest price improvement and a lower cost base rather than from volume: cost of goods sold fell while revenue rose, lifting gross profit to IDR277.3bn and operating profit to IDR224.4bn [S0, S18]. Net profit doubled to IDR159.3bn, or Rp28 a share [S0, S18].

The FY2025 accounts need one restatement. The data pack carries a token depreciation charge because the Indonesian filing uses the direct cash-flow method; the notes show amortisation of mature bearer plants of IDR99.0bn and fixed-asset depreciation of IDR16.0bn, split between cost of sales and G&A [S4, F3, F5]. Total D&A is therefore IDR115.0bn, and the FY2025A da line in the model is restated to that total (FY2024, IDR100.0bn) so the history, the calibration actual and the EV/EBITDA metric all sit on the same basis [S4, F57, F58, F59]. FY2025 EBITDA is IDR339.4bn [S4]. We carry the full charge in the forecast, at about Rp2,600,000 per tonne of CPO in FY2026, rising with the replanted asset base and the revaluation [S4, S10]. Re-priced at FY2025 volume and the FY2025 benchmark, the model now reproduces the LK's FY2025 EBITDA to within one percent: the calibration residual is a small cost-basis difference, not a missing depreciation charge [S4, F5].

FY2025 volume is a proxy, and we label it as one. The FY2025 LK, the annual report and the company's exchange reply carry no annual CPO tonnage, so we hold the FY2024 audited production of 53.1 kt as the denominator; the company did tell the exchange in October 2025 that third-quarter output was above the prior year [S17, S4, F1, F2]. The band is wide — the FY2023 peak was 72.0 kt — but the proxy is the most likely point, not the most cautious: the domestic price implied by the FY2026 plan of Rp14,500/kg is consistent with the FY2024-trough denominator and would be implausibly low at the FY2023 peak [S10, F11, F27]. Because the realisation and the unit cost are both derived from the same revenue and cost totals, the proxy changes per-tonne labels by less than it changes the FY2025 result; the forecast volume is anchored on the 2026 actuals, not on the proxy [S8, S15].

The current year is a tale of two halves, and the second half is a reversal of the first. First-half revenue fell to IDR305.0bn from IDR385.2bn a year earlier, and net profit halved to IDR44.5bn as administrative costs jumped: G&A rose to IDR80.1bn, of which fixed-asset depreciation was IDR42.4bn [S19, S15]. The third quarter reversed sharply: revenue rose to IDR261.0bn, gross profit to IDR91.0bn, and net profit to IDR91.0bn, taking nine-month revenue to IDR566.1bn [S8]. The Q3 bridge is visible in the reported lines: gross profit was IDR91.0bn, the quarterly SG&A line was a credit and depreciation reversed, so EBIT ran above gross profit, and interest and tax then brought net profit back to roughly the gross-profit line [S0, S8, S15]. We treat that credit as a reversal of the first-half overaccrual, not a recurring item: FY2026 SG&A is set at the nine-month normalised ratio of 9.0% and D&A at about Rp2,600,000 per tonne, both above the FY2025 rates [S0, S15, S4].

Our forecast no longer reproduces the June plan, because the plan is already out of reach on the actuals. The company targeted 59.2 kt of CPO sales at Rp14,500/kg and revenue of IDR974.0bn [S10]; nine-month revenue of IDR566.1bn means the fourth quarter would have to deliver the balance of a plan struck before the second-half volume was visible [S8]. We instead set FY2026 volume at the nine-month run-rate of 47.5kt, which with other revenue of about the same annualised PK flow gives FY2026 revenue of IDR836.3bn and net profit of IDR187.0bn, below the company's IDR293.1bn target [S8, S10, S15]. That is the most likely outcome on the evidence, not a haircut: the shortfall is in volume and price relative to a stale plan, and the cost base is reset to what the first nine months actually show [S15, S0].

From FY2027 the model grows volume with the maturing replant and prices CPO off the deck [S24, S4]. Revenue reaches IDR1,002.8bn, EBITDA IDR506.6bn and net profit IDR278.7bn, before flattening as the deck reverts toward its long-run marker [S24]. The cost base is held at the FY2026 run-rate in real terms, with rupiah escalation and no real cost inflation beyond the macro deck, and the royalty line is zero because sales are domestic [S17, S4, S25]. Capital spending follows the company's plan: IDR134.4bn in the current year, dominated by replanting [S10].

Cash generation is the strongest part of the story. FY2025 operating cash flow comfortably exceeded net profit, and free cash flow after IDR134.8bn of capital spending was positive [S0]. The model carries the repayment already visible in the nine months to 30 September, so net debt falls from IDR353.7bn at end-2025 to IDR208.1bn in FY2026, then to IDR35.0bn in FY2027, and turns to net cash only in FY2028 (IDR-151.7bn) [S0]. The fourth quarter is assumed flat after the September repayment rather than repeating it [S0]. Working capital is the offset: operating working capital runs at about a quarter of revenue — IDR242.3bn at end-2025 — and the September balance sheet shows receivables and inventories both higher than at the year-end while cash is minimal [S0].

Capital allocation is conservative on the dividend and heavy on reinvestment. The company paid IDR40.0bn of dividends for FY2025, or Rp7 a share, a payout of about a quarter of net profit, and retained the rest [S11]. There is no buyback and no share issuance in the plan [S4]. The bank facility carries negative covenants, including a restriction on dividend distributions unless the amount is returned as paid-in capital, which we flag as a constraint to monitor [S4].

Earnings quality is mixed. On the positive side, accruals have been strongly negative for three years — cash flow has run ahead of reported profit — which is what a well-run plantation should show [S0]. On the negative side, the FY2026 pattern is less clean. Receivables and inventories built up through the first nine months faster than revenue, the administrative expense line was volatile enough to swing a quarter's profit, and a tax collection letter was received for the May-2025 corporate income-tax period on 19 December 2025 [S0, S4]. The related-party concentration is the dominant flag: 87.7% of FY2025 sales went to JARR and a further IDR96.5bn to Kodeco, so related parties take essentially all revenue; in H1-2026 the share was 97.5%, and JARR's trade receivables to its three related CPO suppliers equal 73.6% of its cost of goods sold [S9, S15, S18, S10]. That is a receivables chain inside one family group, and it is the channel through which value can move away from minority holders.

Two further accounting points matter for anyone rebuilding the numbers. First, the bearer plants and land were revalued under PSAK 16, and a revaluation surplus of IDR683.5bn sits inside FY2025 book equity of IDR1,918.7bn [S4, F48, F49]. Book value therefore overstates historical cost. We do not use P/BV in the valuation: the house card requires pre-revaluation book for any P/BV work, and the filing prints the pre-revaluation base only as components — total equity less the revaluation surplus — rather than as a line we can restate cleanly, so we exclude the method rather than apply it to a book the card rules out [S4, F48, F49]. Second, the archived audited statements in our file do not reproduce the auditor's report pages, so we cannot quote the opinion; the statements carry a directors' statement and are prepared under Indonesian standards [S4]. We treat the absence as an open item for the next update rather than as evidence of a qualification.

A plantation is a depleting, price-taking asset, so we value it on a life-of-asset discounted cash flow at through-cycle prices, cross-checked on EV/EBITDA [S24, S25]. The primary method is a FCFF model to the 2033 HGU expiry, extended by the 25-year extension and 35-year renewal that PP 18/2021 provides for and that ISAK 336 treats as expected, with a terminal value at the deck's long-run CPO marker and rupiah terminal growth below the risk-free rate [S28, S4, S24]. The discount rate is built bottom-up from the macro deck: a rupiah risk-free rate of 7.4%, a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2%, an Indonesia country premium of 2.5% and an industry beta of 0.80, blended with the after-tax cost of debt at the model's marginal gearing [S25].

At a weighted average cost of capital of 11.2%, the DCF gives Rp600 a share, with terminal value 61.2% of the total [S24, S28]. That terminal share is high, and it is the price of valuing a perpetual estate; it is why we cross-check with multiples rather than relying on the DCF alone, and it is bounded by the sourced extension and renewal rather than by an open-ended perpetuity [S28]. The EV/EBITDA cross-check at 6.7 times gives Rp395, -34.2% below the DCF, and the peer-median P/E of 8.2 times gives Rp229, -61.9% below it [S24]. Both multiples use the peer median alone: the own-history leg we used before embedded the same concentrated-ownership premium that the konglo lens is meant to measure separately, so we exclude it rather than import the premium into fundamental value [S26, S24]. P/BV is excluded altogether, because the only book in the pack is the PSAK 16 revalued equity and the house card requires pre-revaluation book for any P/BV work; the pre-revaluation base is not printed as a line, so we drop the method rather than apply the prohibited basis [S4, F48, F49]. The wide DCF-to-multiple gap is the long-run extension value against multiples on today's LTM earnings, which the 2026 cost reset has depressed: the DCF capitalises the extension era, while both multiples capitalise a cyclical and operating low [S25, S4]. The LTM EBITDA in that cross-check is the restated IDR339.4bn, not the pack's amortisation-only figure [S4, F57].

The methods now disagree in a way that matters, and we do not paper over it. The DCF is the high value because it capitalises the extension era; the peer-multiple cross-checks are lower because they apply today's earnings and book to a business whose near-term profit is at a cyclical and operating low. Weighting the DCF at 60.0%, the EBITDA cross-check at 25.0% and the P/E cross-check at 15.0% gives Rp493 [S24, S25]. Rolling that forward twelve months at the cost of equity gives the base-case value of Rp540; probability-weighting the three business scenarios gives Rp520, and applying the 10.0% liquidity discount for a thin float gives a fundamental twelve-month value of Rp468 [S24, S25]. The construction is stated explicitly because the chain is easy to misread: Rp540 is the base case alone, Rp520 is the probability-weighted business-scenario value, and Rp468 is that weighted value after the liquidity discount. The unplanted HGU land is not in the DCF cash flows, so we add it as a bridge item at the LK's land carrying value per hectare for the titled balance net of both the planted area and the plasma estate, which PGUN manages for smallholders rather than owns [S4, F47, F9, F7, F39].

The reverse DCF confirms it. The engine cannot bracket today's price within twice the deck's CPO range, so it reports no implied value: the price is not a commodity-price statement at all [S24]. At Rp8,350 the shares trade on 256.3x FY2026 earnings and 123.9x EV/EBITDA, with a dividend yield of 0.1% [S0]. Those are not multiples of a plantation; they are multiples of a story about control.

That is exactly the case the konglo lens is built for. The lens measures the price against a probability-weighted fundamental value today — across our business scenarios and after the liquidity discount, Rp428 a share — and finds a premium ratio of 19.5 times [S26, S24]. It then assumes that a share of the log gap closes over twelve months, with the closing share set by the name's regime flags: on the exchange's high-concentration list, and with a free-float step due inside the window, the base compression is 40.0% of the log gap [S26]. We hold that base rather than argue for a faster collapse, for three reasons specific to PGUN. First, the 31 March 2027 free-float step requires the controller to place roughly the whole of the gap — about 4.9% of the register, or several times the public float's annual turnover at IDR1,024,175,158.7bn a day — so it cannot be met through the market and must come as a placement, rights issue or transfer; that is a supply event, not a price-discovery event, and it argues for compression, not collapse [S26, F18]. Second, the pledged block gives the group a reason to defend the price: the shares are collateral for a facility the bank values on a 150.0% coverage ratio, so a disorderly fall hurts the controller's own financing before it helps the minority [S6, S12]. Third, the bull regime is a real quarter-weight tail because the collateral incentive cuts both ways: if the group refinances the coal facility without selling PGUN, the premium can persist, and a change of control could even set a tender floor [S12, S26]. The bear regime is the forced-sale path, and it requires both a breach of collateral coverage and a decision by the bank to sell; we give it a quarter, the base half and the bull a quarter [S26, S6].

Applied to the twelve-month fundamental value, the base regime scenario gives Rp2,785, the bear scenario Rp848, and the bull scenario Rp10,604 [S26, S12]. Probability-weighted at one quarter, one half and one quarter, the lens produces our Rp4,256 target, which is still many times fundamental value and -48.9% below the price [S26].

The honest caveat is that the target is highly sensitive to the regime assumptions, not to the plantation. Because the bull scenario carries a quarter of the probability and a positive premium-kept factor, the weighted target sits far above the base-scenario outcome. If the group refinances the coal facility and the float deadline is met without forced sales, the lens's own bull path is above today's price [S12, S26]. We do not think that is the most likely path, but it is why we call the shares SELL on a target that is still a large multiple of what the estate is worth, rather than on a target at value.

The downside risks, ranked by what would move the value, are these. Regulation of ownership concentration is the largest: the exchange has taken high-concentration names out of the IHSG and the main indices, the free-float minimum is rising in steps with a first deadline in March 2027 and a final step in 2028, and MSCI has opened a consultation to reclassify Indonesia as a standalone market with a decision by the end of June 2027 [S26, S22]. For a name whose marginal buyer is an index or a flow, that is a direct hit to the premium, with high likelihood and high impact.

Collateral and related-party risk is second. Nearly the entire register is pledged to Bank Mandiri as security for a group facility used for the coal business, and the bank itself acknowledges that a fall in the collateral shares would test the coverage ratio [S6, S5]. A margin call or forced sale would add supply at exactly the moment the float rule demands more shares in public hands — high impact, moderate likelihood [S6, S26]. Related-party terms are the third: with all sales to JARR and Kodeco and a related receivables chain, pricing or payment terms can be changed inside the group without a minority's consent [S18, S10, S15]. The exposure is direct: one percentage point of price on the JARR contract is worth roughly one percent of FY2026 main-product revenue of IDR748.3bn, and a stretch of the receivable would tie up cash that the thin balance sheet does not have [S0, S10].

A change of control is the event the market has not priced. The 92.4% block is pledged; if the bank enforced and transferred it to a third party, control would change, and under POJK 9/2018 a change of control triggers a mandatory tender offer at the highest average price of the preceding three months or the deal price [S26, F17]. Whether a pledge-enforcement transfer is exempt from that obligation is not settled in the sources we hold, and we flag it as an open legal question rather than assume a floor [S26]. If a tender is required, it could put a floor under the price and make the bull regime more than a tail; if the block passes to another affiliate, the premium structure survives and the minority's position is unchanged [S12, S26].

The business risks are more ordinary. CPO prices can undershoot the deck, and the bear case prices them below it [S24]. The rupiah can move against the cost base, although a weaker rupiah helps revenue [S25]. Weather is a live exposure: the estate is in a fire-prone part of Kalimantan, and the company had to reassure the exchange after the late-2026 fires [S7]. Operational risk is concentrated in one mill: a sustained outage would stop all revenue [S7]. Liquidity is thin, with a small free float and modest daily turnover, so entry and exit are expensive [S0]. Governance is the umbrella over all of it: a family-controlled register, pledged shares, related-party sales and an auditor's report we could not verify from the archived filing [S4, S5].

Our business scenarios are mirrored around the base. The bear case prices CPO below the deck and trims volume, the bull case lifts both by the same magnitude, and the base case holds the deck [S24]. The probabilities are one quarter bear, one half base and one quarter bull, reflecting a genuinely uncertain palm price rather than a cautious tilt [S24].

The konglo regime scenarios are separate and are what set the target. The lens keeps a probability-weighted share of today's premium: the business scenarios value the plantation, then the regime scenarios decide how much of the gap survives twelve months [S26, S24]. The regime catalysts are dated, not vague. The first free-float step falls due on 31 March 2027, with the final step in 2028; the rule is set by the exchange's free-float regulation, and the 2029 outer date reported in some press coverage applies to smaller issuers, not to PGUN's market-cap tier [S26, S21]. MSCI's consultation closes on 30 April 2027 and a decision is due by 30 June 2027 [S22]. The exchange reviews the high-concentration list quarterly. The group's conditional BYAN purchase would, if completed, trigger a mandatory tender offer for BYAN at the highest recent average price or the deal price; it does not by itself create a tender obligation for PGUN, whose only tender path runs through pledge enforcement on its own block [S13, S12, S26].

The signposts that would change our view are specific. A credible sell-down that lifts free float toward the first step without a discount would reduce the forced-supply risk and, perversely, could narrow the gap more slowly than the bear case assumes [S26]. A completed BYAN acquisition financed without further pledges would lower margin-call risk; a further pledge of PGUN or JARR shares would raise it [S6, S12]. A dividend cut, a rights issue at a discount to the market, or a related-party asset purchase would each be a governance signal that the minority's cash flows are being redirected [S11, S10]. And a sustained CPO move well above the deck would lift fundamental value, but the sensitivity table shows how far it would have to go [S24].

Ownership is the defining fact. The Jhonlin group controls PGUN through three family vehicles — Araya Agro Lestari, Citra Agro Raya and Baramega Citra Mulia Persada — which together hold effectively the whole register; the ultimate beneficiary is Liana Saputri, the controller's daughter, and the public holds 7.6% [S11, S12]. The same controller owns JARR, the sole buyer of PGUN's CPO, and the coal and logistics interests that sit behind the group's borrowings [S18, S6]. The exchange has publicly questioned simultaneous price rises across PGUN, JARR and TEBE and asked for explanations of share pledging and margin-call risk [S17, S5]. The name is on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list, is excluded from the IHSG and from LQ45/IDX30/IDX80, and MSCI's standalone consultation threatens passive flows [S26, S13, S22].

Related-party gravity is unusually high even for an Indonesian family group. Sales to JARR are 87.7% of FY2025 revenue and a further IDR96.5bn went to Kodeco, so the two related buyers account for essentially all sales; in H1-2026 the combined share was 97.5%, and JARR's receivables from its three related CPO suppliers are 73.6% of its cost of goods sold [S9, S15, S18, S10]. PGUN also has related-party payables and a shareholder loan in its accounts, and the group's refinancing depends on the same bank that holds the pledged shares [S4, S6]. We quantify this as the single largest source of value leakage: a price set one notch lower on the affiliate contract moves PGUN's cash flow directly, with no market check, and the FY2025 accounts already show the second channel through Kodeco that the earlier JARR-only figure hid [S9, S15].

The share pledge is the sharpest structure flag. 5.3 bn shares of PGUN shares, effectively the whole controlling stake, were pledged to Bank Mandiri as additional collateral for a group credit facility used for the coal business, and the bank has said it tests the collateral against share-price volatility [S5, S6]. The facility documents, as reported by the bank, treat the shares as a secondary way out, but a sustained fall in the collateral price still creates a margin-call mechanism that can put stock into the market [S6]. The company's own response was that the borrower is an affiliate and the pledge is not PGUN's liability, which is true but does not remove the supply risk to shareholders [S5].

The free-float ladder is the other dated structure flag. Public float is 7.6% against a minimum that rises to 15.0%, with the first step to 12.5% required by 31 March 2027 and the final step by 2028; the gap to the first step is 4.9% and the window is about 5.0 months [S26, F18]. The press report of a 2029 outer deadline refers to the exchange's headline transition, not to the tier PGUN sits in; the konglo registry records the 2027 and 2028 dates for a large-cap name below the first-step threshold of 12.5% [S26, S21].

On the board and audit, the published material is thin. The board comprises a president director and a finance director, both named in the filings [S2]. The archived audited statements omit the auditor's report pages, so we could not verify the opinion from the source in our file; there is a directors' statement and the accounts are prepared under Indonesian standards [S4]. That is an evidence gap, not a finding, and it is on our list for the next update. The dividend record is short but real: the company paid IDR40.0bn for FY2025 at Rp7 a share [S11]. The bank facility's negative covenants restrict dividends unless the amount is returned as paid-in capital, a constraint to watch alongside the group's cash needs [S4].

ESG exposure is concentrated in land, fire and smallholder relations. The estate operates under a land title that runs to 2033, with a sourced extension and renewal path under PP 18/2021, and the company has a formal fire-response structure, including patrols, water infrastructure and a no-burn policy, which it activated during the late-2026 Kalimantan fires [S4, S7, S28]. It also manages plasma smallholder blocks covering 3,625 ha, which carry social-license risk if the partnership terms are renegotiated [S4, S8, F39]. We have not found an enforcement action or a sustainability-certification failure in the sources reviewed; the main ESG risk for the equity is not environmental performance but the governance overlay described above [S13, S7].

The dated catalysts are the free-float steps, the MSCI decision and the group's corporate actions. The first free-float step falls due on 31 March 2027 and the final one in 2028; the mechanism — a controller sell-down or new shares — determines whether the premium compresses through supply or dilution [S26]. MSCI's consultation closes on 30 April 2027 and its decision is due by 30 June 2027 [S22]. On the group side, completion of the conditional BYAN purchase would trigger a mandatory tender offer for BYAN and would also tell us how the acquisition is financed; any PGUN tender would come only from pledge enforcement on the PGUN block, not from this deal [S12, S5, S26]. The exchange reviews its high-concentration list quarterly, and any change in index treatment is a flow event for a name this thin [S13, S16]. The HGU expires in 2033, and the extension application under PP 18/2021 is a dated licence event for the terminal value [S4, S28].

Between updates we watch a short list of operating and governance indicators. On the operating side: quarterly CPO production and the volume sold to JARR, the realised price against the deck, the mill's extraction rate, the progress of replanting and the immature-to-mature conversion [S10, S17, S4]. On the financial side: the receivables balance and its ageing, the related-party payable, the cash balance, and the interest cost on the bank facility [S0, S4]. On the governance side: any change in the pledge, any new related-party transaction, any issuance or rights issue, and any exchange query or sanction [S5, S6, S26].

Our rating changes if the price falls toward the lens's base path without a deterioration in the business, or if a credible path to a much higher fundamental value emerges from the estate — neither of which we see in the current deck [S24]. It would also change if the group's ownership structure normalises faster than the lens assumes, for example through a genuine free-float sell-down that removes the forced-supply overhang, or if a change-of-control tender sets a floor above our target [S26, S12].

assumptions.label: Sales volume plan
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is set at the 9M-2026 run-rate, not the stale June plan: 9M revenue of Rp566.1bn [S8] plus a Q4 at the Q4-2025 seasonal share (32% of the year, [S0]) implies about Rp835bn for the year; at the deck price and 0.79 realisation, and with other revenue of Rp88bn, that is about 47.5kt, against the June plan's 59.2kt [S10]. Q1-2026 CPO supplied to JARR was 8.4kt [F21], consistent with the lower run-rate. FY2027-2030 recover at about 6% a year as the 1,617 ha replanted in 2025 and the Rp118.6bn programme mature, reaching 66kt against the 71.956kt peak in 2023 [S20]. FY2025 is a proxy held at the FY2024 audited production because the FY2025 LK, AR and exchange reply carry no annual tonnage [F1, F2, S17].

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: Calibrated on FY2025: CPO revenue of about Rp694.9bn (up 4.18% yoy, [S9]) over 53.108kt [F2] at the FY2025 benchmark of 1,007 USD/t and 16,448 IDR/USD gives 0.79. The discount to the export benchmark is the JARR domestic offtake arrangement [S9, S17], not a forecast-year spike. Cross-checked on 2026: H1 CPO revenue of Rp258.7bn [F44] over the Q1-2026 supply run-rate of 8.4kt [F21] implies a realised price near the deck-based figure and above the June plan's Rp14,500/kg [F11], so 0.79 is held flat rather than fitted to the plan price.

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: Engine default: PGUN sells all CPO domestically under a commercial offtake with JARR [S17]; no DMO-style capped share applies to the group's sales.

assumptions.label: Strip ratio (bcm per tonne) or cost-intensity factor
assumptions.basis: Palm oil cost intensity is expressed per tonne of CPO, so the intensity factor is 1.0 and all cash cost sits in cost_per_bcm; there is no overburden analogue in a plantation.

assumptions.label: Cash cost per tonne of CPO (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: Set at the 9M-2026 run-rate: 9M COGS of Rp325.7bn (H1 Rp155.6bn [F32] plus Q3 COGS implied by the Rp90.97bn gross profit [F46] on Rp261.1bn revenue [S0]), less H1 depreciation of Rp42.43bn [F43] and the by-product cost of about Rp67bn of PK, leaves about Rp260bn, or about Rp7.2m per tonne at the 47.5kt run-rate. Held in real terms with 2.5% IDR escalation, no real cost inflation beyond the macro deck [S25].

assumptions.label: Fuel share of mining cost
assumptions.basis: Engine default scalar; the fuel driver is empty for PLANTATIONS so the fuel term does not enter the cost build.

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit (haul, barge, process)
assumptions.basis: Haul, milling and port costs are already inside the per-tonne CPO cash cost backed out of the FY2025 LK [S0, S4]; no separate unit line is added to avoid double counting.

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat regimes)
assumptions.basis: Zero: all CPO is marketed domestically to affiliated JARR [S17, S9] and Indonesia's CPO export levy is borne by the exporter at shipment, not by PGUN on a domestic sale. The FY2025 COGS note carries no royalty or export-levy line [S4].

assumptions.label: Other revenue (PK and shells)
assumptions.basis: Set at the 2026 run-rate, not the June plan: H1-2026 PK revenue was Rp46.28bn [F45] and Q3/Q4 run at a similar level, giving about Rp88bn for the year against the plan's Rp115.6bn [S10]. It grows with PK output and IDR prices thereafter, against Rp97.7bn of FY2025 PK and shell revenue [S9].

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: PK and shells are by-products of FFB already milled for CPO; about 65% margin after the incremental pressing and handling cost, consistent with Rp96bn of FY2025 PK revenue against a thin incremental cost base [S9].

assumptions.label: D&A per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 total non-cash charge is Rp115.0bn: bearer-plant amortisation Rp99.0bn [F3] plus fixed-asset depreciation Rp16.0bn [F5] (Rp11.66bn in COGS [F50] and the balance in G&A), about Rp2.17m per tonne on 53.108kt. H1-2026 G&A depreciation alone was Rp42.43bn [F43], but the third-quarter accounts reversed the overaccrual [S0]; we carry Rp2.6m/t in FY2026, above the FY2025 rate and consistent with the revalued asset base and replanting programme [S4, S10].

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: FY2026 plan of Rp167.61bn over 59.2kt is Rp2.83m per tonne, including Rp118.6bn of replanting [S10]; held in real terms with 2.5% IDR escalation, consistent with FY2025 actual capex of Rp134.77bn (Rp2.54m/t) [S0].

assumptions.label: Other capex (expansion projects)
assumptions.basis: Engine default zero: the FY2026 plan is sustaining and replanting capex and no separately budgeted expansion project is disclosed [S10].

The FY2026 entry carries that nine-month repayment to the reporting date and assumes the fourth quarter is flat, so the model's FY2026 debt matches the September balance rather than assuming a second Rp100bn paydown; FY2027 carries a further Rp20bn, then flat as capex and dividends absorb free cash flow.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Engine default zero: no issuance or buyback is planned and the 5,737.85m shares are unchanged in the FY2025 LK [F6].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House old-currency terminal growth: 4% nominal IDR, below the 7.45% IDR risk-free rate and above the macro deck's 2.5% long-run IDR inflation, so terminal value assumes no perpetual real premium on top of volume growth.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Set on the 9M-2026 normalised run-rate: H1-2026 G&A of Rp80.11bn [F42] less the Q3 credit of Rp28.8bn disclosed in the pack [S0] gives about Rp51.3bn on Rp566.1bn revenue, or 9.1%. FY2025 was 6.67% [S9]; the H1 spike and its Q3 reversal bracket the two, and 9.0% is the most likely normalised ratio, held flat in percentage terms.

challenges.challenge: The FY2025A EBITDA is rebuilt on bearer-plant amortisation alone. The `da` fact is F3 99.016bn, so the model prints EBITDA 323.43 (EBIT 224.41 + 99.02). The LK also charges fixed-asset depreciation of 16.019bn (F5: 11.656bn in cost of sales and 4.363bn in G&A), so total D&A is 115.035bn and the comparable EBITDA is 339.45bn. That "actual" is what the calibration gate compares and what the EV/EBITDA cross-check capitalises (323.43 x 13.557), so both are computed on an understated base. Worse, the gate's third justification clause - "F3 carries only bearer-plant amortisation while the forecast adds fixed-asset depreciation" - cannot explain an EBITDA gap at all: in the model's own formula EBITDA = revenue - cash cost - other COGS - opex, and da cancels. S15 shows H1-2026 G&A depreciation alone at 42.43bn (vs 1.01bn), so the forecast da_unit of 2.2m/t (130.2bn) is also below the current run-rate.
challenges.answer: FY2025 and FY2024 are now stated on total D&A: bearer-plant amortisation F3/F4 plus fixed-asset depreciation F5/F59 (F5 split between COGS F50 and G&A in note 14). The da facts themselves are now the totals (F57 115.035 for FY2025A, F58 100.046 for FY2024A), derived from the quoted components with the addition disclosed in the labels because the LK prints no combined line; the engine's da line, calibration actual and EV/EBITDA metric all use 115.035 and FY2025 EBITDA is 339.4bn. Re-priced at FY2025 volume and benchmark the calibration gap is 0.9%, not a definitional mismatch. The forecast da_unit stays at 2.6m/t, above the FY2025 rate and below the H1-2026 G&A run-rate after its Q3 reversal.

challenges.challenge: Every input that drives the valuation is cited [S0], which the analyst card defines as the Yahoo data pack, to be cited for reported financials only. S0 cannot contain the house agri deck (FY2026E 1,135, FY2027E 1,240, LT 1,150, spot 1,180 USD/t), the macro deck (IDR/USD, inflation, risk-free), or the WACC build. The deck's own archived sources (fund record S1-S9, including the Kemendag Harga Referensi and the FCPO strip) are not registered for this ticker. The largest lever in the report - the CPO price path - therefore has no source a reader can open, in contrast to the AADI and JARR initiations, which cite deck facts to the deck's S#s rather than S0.
challenges.answer: The house agri deck, macro deck and konglo registry/regime deck are now registered as sources S24, S25 and S26 (kind data, asof recorded), and the PP 18/2021 text is S28. Every deck, macro and WACC sentence now cites the deck source, not S0; S0 is reserved for PGUN's reported financials and market data.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E revenue is 1,048.25bn against the company's own plan of 973.96bn [S10], +7.6%, and the whole difference is price: the model values 59.2kt at about Rp15,750/kg (deck 1,135 USD/t x 0.79 x 17,570) where the plan uses Rp14,500/kg. The stated reason - "the plan was struck in June and palm prices have since moved" - cites [S10, S0] and neither source says it. The pack can test the price: H1-2026 CPO revenue was Rp258.7bn [S15] and Q1 supply 8.4kt [S10], so the realised price is derivable, but the report does not show it. Keeping the plan volume with a price the plan does not use is a hybrid, not the company's plan.
challenges.answer: FY2026 is no longer the June plan with a deck price. Nine-month revenue of Rp566.1bn and the Q4-2025 seasonal share imply about Rp835bn for the year; at the deck price and 0.79 realisation, with other revenue at the annualised PK flow, that is 47.5kt, not 59.2kt. H1-2026 CPO revenue of Rp258.7bn over the Q1-2026 supply of 8.4kt implies a realised price near the deck-based figure and above the plan's Rp14,500/kg, so the plan price, not the deck price, was the outlier. FY2026 revenue, EBITDA, net profit and DPS all move with the restated volume; the report states the shortfall against the company target and does not hybridise plan volume with a non-plan price.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E net profit (292.36bn) sits at the company's 293.15bn target, but 9M-2026 NP is only 135.5bn (H1 44.51 + Q3 91.0), requiring Q4 of 157bn, +72% on Q3. Q3 is not a clean quarter: its net profit (91.0bn) equals its gross profit (90.97bn [S8]), so opex, finance cost and tax were netted to zero by a credit or other income the sources do not identify. The report asserts "the administrative line swung from a large first-half charge to a credit" citing [S0, S19]; S19 covers H1 only and S0 is Yahoo. The cost base also ignores the observed run-rate: H1-2026 G&A was 80.11bn, of which 42.43bn depreciation [S15], so cash G&A was 37.7bn, 12.4% of revenue, against a FY2025 cash-opex ratio of 6.1%, while the model holds opex_pct at 6.67% in every year.
challenges.answer: The Q3 bridge is now stated line by line from the reported pack and press: gross profit Rp90.97bn, the quarterly SG&A line as a credit and depreciation reversing, EBIT above gross profit, then interest and tax bringing net profit back to the gross-profit line. We treat the credit as the reversal of the H1 overaccrual and normalise: SG&A at the 9M ratio of 9.0% (H1 G&A Rp80.11bn less the Q3 credit on Rp566.1bn 9M revenue) and D&A at 2.6m/t, above FY2025. FY2026E is restated to the run-rate, not kept at the company target. S15 is cited.

challenges.challenge: The report treats 87.66% as the related-party share of sales. That is JARR only. S9 also records Rp96.46bn of FY2025 revenue from PT Kodeco Agrojaya Mandiri, which PGUN itself calls a related party on a family/commissioner link; S15 reports that 97.55% of H1-2026 revenue came from JARR and Kodeco, "dua entitas di bawah kendali Jhonlin Group"; S10 names Kodeco as one of JARR's three related CPO suppliers. On the FY2025 disclosures related-party sales are ~99.8% of revenue (694.9 + 96.46 of 792.7), not 87.7%. The central governance channel in the bear case is understated by ~12pp, and F16's "sales to the controlling group (JARR)" label hides the second channel.
challenges.answer: The Kodeco flow is now a fact (F40, Rp96.46bn FY2025) and the H1-2026 combined related-party share is F41 (97.55%). §3 and §6 state that JARR's 87.66% is the JARR-only channel and that JARR plus Kodeco take essentially all revenue; the F16 label is corrected. We size the channel by noting that one percentage point of price on the JARR contract is about one percent of FY2026 main-product revenue, and that the receivable stretch ties up cash the balance sheet does not have.

challenges.challenge: The konglo base case closing 40% of a 14.1x log gap in twelve months is asserted from the flags, not argued for this name, which VAL_KONGLO §4 requires. The arithmetic in the pack points the other way: the first free-float step needs 4.88pp, about 280m shares (64% of the 437m public float), worth ~Rp2.34tn at Rp8,350, against the model's ADTV of Rp1.02bn/day (~123k shares/day) - roughly 2,280 trading sessions. The 31-Mar-2027 deadline cannot be met through the market; it needs a discounted placement, a rights issue or a transfer, all of which add supply or dilute. The collateral runs the same way: S12 values the pledged block at a 50% haircut and S6 puts the CCR at 150% on Rp17tn drawn, so a move toward the lens's own base (3,162) or bear (1,096) breaches coverage and forces the sale the bear describes. The bull regime (25% probability, +25% on today's price) assumes the controller supports the stock while pledging it, with no source.
challenges.answer: §4 now argues the 40% base for PGUN specifically: the first free-float step needs about 4.88pp of the register, several times the public float's annual turnover at the reported ADTV, so it cannot be met through the market and must be a placement, rights issue or transfer; the pledged block gives the controller a defence incentive because the collateral is tested on a 150% coverage ratio; and the bull regime is a real quarter-weight tail because refinancing without a sell-down, or a tender floor on a change of control, can preserve the premium. The bear is the forced-sale path and needs both a coverage breach and a bank decision to sell. The lens parameters are the deck's; we argue the probability rather than re-fit it.

challenges.challenge: The DCF discounts ten years (FY2026-FY2035) plus a terminal value at 4% growth, and the TV is 51.8% of value, but the HGU runs only to 2033 with an option to extend [S4 p.17]. FY2034-35 and the whole perpetuity therefore sit beyond the licence in the base case; no extension is sourced, costed or risked, and §1 states the 2033 expiry while §4 never mentions it.
